title: Wellbutrin and Alcohol: Seizure Risk, Tolerance, and Safe Limits
excerpt: Can you drink on Wellbutrin (bupropion)? Why alcohol and bupropion both affect seizure risk, what the label says, XL and Zyban, reduced tolerance, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Can you drink on Wellbutrin? How bupropion and alcohol affect seizure risk, what the label says, XL and Zyban, feeling drunk faster, and when to get help.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Wellbutrin (bupropion) is one of the antidepressants where alcohol matters most, and the reason is different from most other medicines. The main concern isn't drowsiness or liver strain. It's **seizures**. Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold, which means it makes the brain somewhat easier to tip into a seizure, and alcohol can push on that same threshold, especially when someone drinks heavily or suddenly stops after a stretch of regular drinking. The official prescribing information tells people to minimize or avoid alcohol while taking it. Many people on Wellbutrin do have an occasional drink without trouble, but whether that's reasonable for *you* depends on your dose, your drinking pattern, and your health history, which is a conversation to have with the doctor who prescribed it.

**The quick rules:** Don't start, stop, or skip Wellbutrin doses to make room for drinking. Don't binge drink on it. If you drink most days and want to cut back or stop, don't quit alcohol suddenly without talking to a doctor first, because stopping abruptly is one of the situations the label specifically flags. If you do drink, keep it light, slow, and with food, and pay attention to whether alcohol hits you harder than it used to. If someone on bupropion has a seizure, call 911.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and the official prescribing information for bupropion. It is not a substitute for the doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history and your full medication list. **Talk to your doctor before drinking on Wellbutrin if** you've ever had a seizure, a head injury, or an eating disorder, you drink most days, you take other medicines that lower the seizure threshold, or you're on a higher dose. **Call 911 if** someone on bupropion has a seizure, becomes unresponsive, or has trouble breathing. If you notice new or worsening thoughts of suicide or self-harm, contact your doctor right away, or call or text **988** (the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline in the US).

## Why Wellbutrin and Alcohol Don't Mix: The Seizure-Threshold Problem in Plain Words

Wellbutrin is a brand name. The drug inside it is **bupropion**. It's prescribed for depression, for seasonal depression, and, under the brand name **Zyban**, to help people quit smoking. It's also one half of the weight-loss medicine **Contrave** (bupropion plus naltrexone).

Bupropion works differently from the more common antidepressants like Zoloft or Lexapro. Those are SSRIs, which act mainly on serotonin. Bupropion is often described as an NDRI, meaning it mostly affects two other brain chemicals, **dopamine and norepinephrine**. That's why it tends to feel more activating than sedating, and why it's less likely to cause the sexual side effects or weight gain some people get on SSRIs.

The trade-off is that bupropion carries a known, dose-related risk of seizures. Every brain has a "seizure threshold," a level of electrical excitability above which a seizure can happen. Most of the time, ours sits comfortably below it. Bupropion nudges the brain closer to that line. At normal doses in people without other risk factors, the chance of a seizure is low, and the prescribing information lists rates on the order of roughly 1 in 1,000 at standard doses. But the risk climbs with higher doses and with anything else that also pushes the brain toward that threshold.

### How alcohol pushes on the same threshold

Alcohol affects seizure risk in a way that surprises a lot of people, because it works in two directions over time:

- **While you're drinking, alcohol calms the brain.** It boosts GABA (the brain's main "slow down" signal) and dampens glutamate (a main "speed up" signal). In the moment, that's a depressant effect.
- **When alcohol wears off, the brain rebounds.** If you drink heavily, or drink regularly enough that your brain adapts, the brain compensates by turning its own excitability up. When the alcohol leaves, that turned-up state is left unopposed. This rebound is what drives alcohol withdrawal, and in its more serious forms it can include **withdrawal seizures**.

Now add bupropion, which is already lowering the threshold. The overlap is clearest in that rebound window: after a binge, or when someone who drinks every day suddenly stops. That's why the bupropion label doesn't just say "alcohol is bad." It specifically calls out **excessive alcohol use and abrupt stopping of alcohol** as situations that can raise seizure risk, and it lists people who are abruptly discontinuing alcohol (or sedatives like benzodiazepines) among those who shouldn't take bupropion at all.

### The part most articles get wrong

A lot of online advice treats this as "one drink on Wellbutrin can give you a seizure." That's not what the evidence or the label describes. The concern is concentrated in a few specific situations: **heavy drinking, binge drinking, and suddenly stopping after regular heavy use**, plus higher doses and other personal risk factors. On the other side, some people read that and conclude alcohol is fine as long as they don't binge. That's not quite right either. The label still advises minimizing or avoiding alcohol, there are reports of people tolerating alcohol unusually poorly on bupropion, and alcohol can work against the very thing the medicine is treating. The honest middle is that light, occasional drinking is a decision to make with your prescriber, not something to assume is safe or unsafe for everyone.

## What the Prescribing Information and Research Actually Say

This is one of the better-documented alcohol warnings among antidepressants, because the seizure issue has been part of bupropion's story since the beginning.

**Seizure risk shaped how the drug is sold.** Bupropion was first approved in the US in the 1980s, and its launch was delayed after seizures were seen in early studies, particularly in a trial involving patients with eating disorders. The drug came back with lower maximum doses, split dosing, and later the slow-release versions (SR and XL), partly to keep peak blood levels lower and the seizure risk down.

**The label tells people to minimize or avoid alcohol.** The US prescribing information for bupropion products advises patients to minimize or avoid drinking. It also explains that excessive use or abrupt discontinuation of alcohol or sedatives can increase the risk of seizures.

**The label mentions reduced alcohol tolerance.** The prescribing information notes rare post-marketing reports of adverse neuropsychiatric events or **reduced alcohol tolerance** in people who drank while taking bupropion. That matches a common experience people describe online: feeling drunk faster, or getting a stronger reaction to amounts they used to handle. These are reports, not a measured rate, but they're worth taking seriously.

**Several groups can't take bupropion at all.** The label lists contraindications that include a seizure disorder, a current or past diagnosis of bulimia or anorexia, and people undergoing abrupt discontinuation of alcohol, benzodiazepines, barbiturates, or antiseizure medicines. The alcohol entry is there for the reason described above: the withdrawal window and bupropion's effect on the threshold overlap.

**Interestingly, bupropion has been studied as a treatment for drinking problems.** Because it acts on dopamine, researchers have looked at whether it reduces alcohol cravings, and the naltrexone half of Contrave is itself a drug used for alcohol use disorder. The results for bupropion alone haven't been strong enough to make it a standard treatment for drinking. It's a good reminder that the relationship between this drug and alcohol is complicated, and that the research question "does it help people drink less" is separate from "is it safe to drink on it."

## Can You Drink on Wellbutrin at All?

Here's how the risk generally breaks down. These are broad categories to help you have a better conversation with your doctor, not personal advice.

| Situation | General picture |
|---|---|
| No drinking | The lowest-risk option and what the label leans toward. |
| An occasional single drink, with food, on a stable dose | Many prescribers consider this lower risk for people without other seizure risk factors, but ask yours first. Watch for reduced tolerance. |
| Several drinks in one sitting (binge drinking) | Higher concern. This is one of the patterns the label flags as "excessive." |
| Drinking most days, then stopping suddenly | Highest concern. Abrupt alcohol withdrawal is a listed contraindication for bupropion. Get medical guidance before stopping. |
| Higher doses, past seizure, head injury, eating disorder | Extra risk factors that stack. Ask your doctor before any drinking. |

A few practical points if your doctor is fine with occasional light drinking:

- **One drink means one standard drink.** That's about 12 ounces of regular beer, 5 ounces of wine, or 1.5 ounces of liquor. Many cocktails and craft beers are more than one.
- **Go slowly and eat.** Food slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood, which keeps peaks lower.
- **Try a smaller amount than usual the first time.** Because of reports of reduced tolerance, it's sensible to find out how you react with one drink rather than three.
- **Don't drink to manage how you feel.** If you notice you're reaching for alcohol to deal with low mood, anxiety, or sleep, that's useful information to bring to your prescriber.

## Bupropion and Alcohol: Does the Generic Behave Differently?

No. **Bupropion and Wellbutrin are the same drug.** Wellbutrin is the original brand; bupropion is the generic name, and generic versions contain the same active ingredient at the same strengths. Everything in this article about alcohol applies equally to brand-name Wellbutrin, generic bupropion, and other brand names it's sold under (such as Aplenzin, which is a different salt form of bupropion).

The one thing that can differ between products is the release form, which affects how the dose is spread over the day. That's covered next.

## Wellbutrin XL and Alcohol: Does the Version Matter?

Bupropion comes in three main forms:

- **IR (immediate release):** the original version, taken several times a day. Rarely used now.
- **SR (sustained release):** usually taken twice a day.
- **XL (extended release):** taken once a day, usually in the morning.

The slower-release versions were designed partly to smooth out blood levels and avoid high peaks, since peaks are linked to seizure risk. That's helpful, but **it doesn't make alcohol safe on XL.** The same label warnings about minimizing or avoiding alcohol and about abrupt alcohol withdrawal apply to Wellbutrin XL and SR as well as the older form.

Two XL-specific points that come up a lot:

- **Never crush, chew, or split an XL or SR tablet** unless your pharmacist says that specific product can be split. Breaking the coating can release the dose all at once, which is exactly the kind of peak the slow-release design avoids.
- **Higher doses carry more risk.** Wellbutrin XL is commonly prescribed at 150 mg or 300 mg a day, with 450 mg a day as the usual upper limit. If you're on the higher end, be more careful with alcohol, not less.

## Zyban and Alcohol: Quitting Smoking on Bupropion

**Zyban is bupropion** sold for smoking cessation, so the same alcohol cautions apply. There's a practical wrinkle here, though. For many people, drinking and smoking go together. A night out with a few drinks is one of the most common times people slip and have a cigarette when they're trying to quit.

That makes the weeks on Zyban a good time to drink less for two reasons at once: the seizure-threshold concern, and protecting your quit attempt. If you're using Zyban, it's worth asking your doctor whether to hold off on drinking entirely while you're getting through the hardest part of quitting.

The same goes for **Contrave**, the weight-loss medicine that combines bupropion with naltrexone. It carries bupropion's seizure warnings and its alcohol caution, and naltrexone adds its own considerations. If you take Contrave, ask your prescriber about alcohol specifically rather than relying on general Wellbutrin advice.

## What People Report on Reddit: Feeling Drunk Faster, Blackouts, and Bad Hangovers

If you search "Wellbutrin and alcohol Reddit," you'll find a lot of personal stories. These aren't research, and you can't tell from a forum post what dose someone was on, what else they took, or how much they really drank. But a few themes come up so often that they're worth addressing honestly.

**"I get drunk way faster on Wellbutrin."** This lines up with the label's mention of reduced alcohol tolerance. It's not well understood why it happens in some people, but it's a good reason to start with less than you'd normally drink and to never assume your old limits still apply.

**"I blacked out after a normal amount."** Blackouts happen when blood alcohol rises high enough or fast enough to stop the brain from forming new memories. If bupropion lowers your tolerance, a familiar amount could put you in that range. A blackout on a "normal" night is a signal to stop and talk to your doctor, not to shrug it off. It's also unsafe in its own right, since people make risky decisions and get hurt during blackouts.

**"My hangovers are brutal now."** People report heavier hangovers, more next-day anxiety, and worse sleep. Bupropion can already cause insomnia and jitteriness in some people, and alcohol fragments sleep and causes a rebound of anxiety as it wears off. Stacking the two can make the next day feel worse. Our guide on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) explains the sleep side of this.

**"I had one drink and nothing happened."** This is common too, and it's part of why the internet feels so contradictory. Most people on standard doses who have a single drink don't have a seizure. That doesn't make heavier drinking safe, and it doesn't mean the next person will react the same way.

The useful takeaway from all of these stories is the same: if alcohol feels noticeably different on bupropion, believe that and adjust, and tell your prescriber.

## Shaking or Feeling Off the Morning After: Know the Difference

This is the section that matters most if you drink regularly.

A normal hangover can include mild shakiness, a racing heart, sweating, and anxiety. Our guides to [hangover shakes](/never-hungover/hangover-shakes) and [a racing heart after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking) cover those everyday versions. For most social drinkers, these settle as the day goes on.

But for someone who's been drinking heavily most days, those same symptoms can be early **alcohol withdrawal**, and withdrawal is exactly the window where bupropion's seizure risk and alcohol's rebound overlap. Signs that point toward withdrawal rather than an ordinary hangover include:

- Symptoms that start or get worse as the alcohol wears off, especially after several days of heavy drinking
- Tremor that keeps getting stronger instead of fading
- Feeling the need to drink to make the shakes stop
- Confusion, seeing or hearing things that aren't there, or severe agitation

**If you drink most days and want to cut back or stop, talk to a doctor before you do it,** and tell them you take bupropion. This isn't about judging how much you drink. It's that stopping suddenly is a specific risk the label names, and a doctor can help you do it safely.

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help Right Away

**Call 911 if someone on bupropion:**

- Has a seizure (stiffening, jerking, loss of consciousness, or a sudden period of staring and unresponsiveness)
- Can't be woken, or is breathing very slowly or irregularly
- Becomes severely confused or has hallucinations after drinking or after stopping drinking

While you wait, move hard or sharp objects out of the way, turn the person onto their side if they're vomiting or after the jerking stops, and don't put anything in their mouth.

**Contact your doctor promptly if you notice:**

- New or worsening depression, anxiety, panic, agitation, or irritability
- Unusual changes in mood or behavior, or thoughts of suicide or self-harm (antidepressants, including bupropion, carry a boxed warning about this, particularly in children and young adults)
- Blackouts, feeling much drunker than expected, or other strong reactions to alcohol
- Persistent racing heart or very high blood pressure readings, which bupropion can raise in some people

If you're in crisis or thinking about harming yourself, call or text **988** in the US, or go to the nearest emergency room.

## Alcohol Can Work Against the Medicine Itself

The seizure issue gets most of the attention, but there's a quieter reason doctors discourage drinking on any antidepressant: **alcohol is a depressant, and it can undo some of what the medicine is trying to do.**

In the short term, a drink can feel like it lifts your mood or eases anxiety. As it wears off, that often reverses, with a dip in mood, more anxiety, and broken sleep. For someone being treated for depression, that pattern can blur the picture. It can make it look like the medicine isn't working when alcohol is part of the problem, or make it harder for you and your doctor to judge whether a dose change is needed. Our article on [alcohol and anxiety](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-anxiety-breaking-the-cycle-naturally-2025) goes deeper into that rebound cycle.

That doesn't mean you've done something wrong if you've had drinks while on Wellbutrin. It means it's worth being honest with your prescriber about how much you drink, so the two of you can make sense of how you're feeling.

## Missed Doses, Timing, and Other Common Questions

**Should you skip your dose to drink?** No. Skipping or stopping doses to "make room" for alcohol isn't a recognized safety strategy, and it can bring back depression symptoms. Missing doses and then restarting can also make your blood levels uneven. If you want to drink and you're not sure how to fit it around your medicine, ask your prescriber rather than adjusting it yourself.

**Should you double up if you missed a dose after a night out?** No. Doubling a bupropion dose raises the peak level in your blood, which is exactly what you want to avoid for seizure risk. Take the next dose at the normal time, or follow your pharmacist's instructions for missed doses.

**Does timing your drink away from your dose help?** XL is designed to keep fairly steady levels across the day, so spacing a drink a few hours from your morning pill doesn't take you "off" the medicine. Timing isn't a substitute for keeping the amount small.

**What about other medicines?** Some drugs also lower the seizure threshold or interact with bupropion, including certain other antidepressants, antipsychotics, some stimulants, tramadol, and theophylline. Bupropion can also raise levels of some medicines processed by the liver enzyme CYP2D6. If you take anything else, including over-the-counter sleep aids or cold medicines that you might reach for after drinking, run it past a pharmacist. Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers how supplements fit into this.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

You're at higher risk from the bupropion-and-alcohol combination if you:

- Drink **most days**, binge drink, or are planning to stop drinking after a period of regular heavy use
- Have ever had a **seizure**, a serious **head injury**, a brain tumor, or a stroke
- Have, or have had, **bulimia or anorexia**
- Are on a **higher dose**, or recently had your dose increased
- Take **other medicines that lower the seizure threshold** or affect how bupropion is processed
- Use **sedatives such as benzodiazepines** and are cutting back on them

If any of these apply, have a direct conversation with your doctor about alcohol before your next drink. A good prescriber won't lecture you; they'll want an accurate picture so they can keep you safe.

## A Better Path: Drink Less, and Support Your Body If You Do

If you're on Wellbutrin and you drink, the single most effective step is the simple one: **drink less, drink slower, and eat and hydrate properly.** For many people the best move during treatment is to take a break from alcohol, at least until they know how they respond. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence for the times you do drink.

Some people also look at supplements. Here's an honest view, with the medication caveat first:

- **Check with your prescriber or pharmacist before adding any supplement** while you take bupropion, since some supplements affect mood, sleep, or seizure risk.
- **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the evidence comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data. There is no good evidence that DHM lowers the seizure risk of combining alcohol with bupropion, and it does not make drinking on Wellbutrin safe. If your doctor is comfortable with occasional light drinking and you want to try it for the morning after, popular picks include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

One rule overrides everything else: no supplement should change how you take your medicine or how much you drink on it. The label's advice to minimize or avoid alcohol stands no matter what else you take.

## The Bottom Line

- Wellbutrin (bupropion) lowers the seizure threshold, and alcohol, especially heavy drinking and sudden stopping, can push on that same threshold. That's the core interaction.
- The prescribing information advises minimizing or avoiding alcohol and lists abrupt alcohol withdrawal as a reason not to take bupropion.
- Generic bupropion, Wellbutrin XL and SR, Zyban, and Contrave all carry the same basic alcohol caution.
- Many people report feeling drunk faster on bupropion. Start with less than you'd expect, and take blackouts or strong reactions seriously.
- Don't skip or double doses around drinking. If you drink most days and want to stop, get medical guidance first.
- If someone on bupropion has a seizure, call 911. If you have thoughts of self-harm, call or text 988.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol on Wellbutrin?**

The prescribing information advises minimizing or avoiding alcohol while taking Wellbutrin (bupropion), mainly because both bupropion and alcohol can affect seizure risk. The risk is highest with heavy drinking, binge drinking, and suddenly stopping after regular heavy use. Some prescribers are comfortable with an occasional single drink for people without other risk factors, but that's a decision to make with your own doctor.

**Can one drink on Wellbutrin cause a seizure?**

For most people on standard doses without other risk factors, a single drink is unlikely to cause a seizure. The label's concern centers on excessive drinking and abrupt alcohol withdrawal, plus higher doses and personal risk factors such as a past seizure, head injury, or eating disorder. That doesn't make any amount risk-free, so ask your prescriber what's reasonable for you.

**Is bupropion and alcohol different from Wellbutrin and alcohol?**

No. Bupropion is the generic name for the drug in Wellbutrin, so the alcohol cautions are the same. That's also true for Wellbutrin XL, Wellbutrin SR, Zyban (bupropion for quitting smoking), and Contrave (bupropion plus naltrexone for weight loss).

**Is Wellbutrin XL safer with alcohol than other forms?**

Not meaningfully. The extended-release design smooths out blood levels, which helps keep seizure risk lower than the old immediate-release form, but the same label warnings about alcohol apply to XL and SR. Never crush or chew an XL or SR tablet, since that can release the dose all at once.

**Why do I get drunk faster on Wellbutrin?**

The prescribing information mentions rare reports of reduced alcohol tolerance in people who drank while taking bupropion, and many people describe feeling drunk faster or having blackouts after familiar amounts. The reason isn't fully understood. If it happens to you, drink less or not at all, and tell your prescriber.

**Should I skip my Wellbutrin dose if I'm going to drink?**

No. Skipping doses to make room for alcohol isn't a recognized safety strategy and can bring back depression symptoms. Don't double up on a missed dose either, since that raises your peak blood level. Ask your prescriber how to handle drinking with your specific dose instead of adjusting it yourself.

**Can I drink alcohol while taking Zyban to quit smoking?**

Zyban is bupropion, so the same advice to minimize or avoid alcohol applies. Drinking is also one of the most common triggers for slipping back into smoking, so many people find it helps their quit attempt to skip alcohol while they're on Zyban. Check with your doctor about what's right for you.

**What should I do if I drink every day and want to stop while on Wellbutrin?**

Talk to a doctor before you stop, and tell them you take bupropion. Suddenly stopping alcohol after regular heavy use can cause withdrawal, which can include seizures, and abrupt alcohol withdrawal is a listed contraindication for bupropion. A doctor can help you cut back safely. If you or someone else has a seizure, call 911.

**Does DHM make it safe to drink on Wellbutrin?**

No. There is no good evidence that DHM reduces the seizure risk of combining alcohol with bupropion. DHM has promising research on alcohol metabolism and liver health, mostly from animal studies with limited human data. Check with your prescriber before adding any supplement, and follow the label's alcohol advice regardless.
